subject: astronomy

moments.title: Cecilia Payne's PhD thesis
moments.body: Payne's PhD thesis 'Stellar Atmospheres' applies Meghnad Saha's ionisation theory to stellar spectra and concludes that stars are overwhelmingly composed of hydrogen and helium — not, as accepted wisdom held, of the same elemental mix as Earth. Henry Norris Russell pressures her to call the result 'spurious'. He retracts four years later, after independent confirmation.

quote.text: The most brilliant PhD thesis ever written in astronomy.

moments.takeaway: A 24-year-old woman discovered what stars are made of. She was forced to disavow her own correct result and watched a male astronomer claim credit.

now.title: Stellar composition today
now.body: Hydrogen ~74% by mass, helium ~24%, everything else <2% — Payne was right. Stellar nucleosynthesis (Burbidge, Burbidge, Fowler, Hoyle 1957, 'B²FH') traces heavier elements to stars. We are made of star-stuff. Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin became Harvard's first female full professor in 1956 — 31 years after her thesis.
now.open_questions: How metal-poor were the first stars? JWST observations of high-redshift galaxies are pushing the boundary.

reflection: Russell's 1929 paper confirming Payne's hydrogen-dominance result is one of the most-cited papers in astronomy. Payne is mentioned in a footnote.
